citation: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging.

We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline.
Rather than interpreting model weights as posterior probabilities, stacking selects weights to maximize out-of-sample predictive performance.
where the goal is not to recover a true model but to construct a predictive ensemble that remains robust under misspecification

In this paper, we take the model-generation step of LLB as given and focus instead on how the resulting collection of candidate models should be aggregated.
Since LLB generates models using a language model, there is no reason to expect that the true model lies within the candidate set.

For each task, we generate 250 candidate NumPyro programs using Qwen2.5 Coder 32B.
Programs are generated from the textual description t alone, deduplicated by normalized code hash, and filtered to retain only those that compile and pass shape validation.
We compare the original LLB evidence-based aggregation rule with the KL-regularized stacking objective introduced in Section 4.
The KL term stabilizes optimization by encouraging proximity to the BMA weights while allowing deviations when supported by predictive performance.
We select λ from a small grid using validation predictive performance on a held-out validation split.
We optimize this objective in log-space using SciPy’s BFGS with softmax parameterization
Predictive performance is measured using expected log predictive density (ELPD) on held-out test data (Vehtari et al., 2017), where higher values indicate better generalization.

This supports the interpretation that the primary difference between the two approaches is not predictive power, but rather the representation of model uncertainty.
This supports our main claim: in language-generated model spaces, the goal is not to identify a single dominant model, but to maintain a meaningful mixture over plausible misspecified candidates.
At the same time, our experiments do not establish that the learned weights recover the true epistemic uncertainty of the data-generating process.
The resulting mixture still depends on the quality and diversity of candidate models generated by the language model.
